parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan ancoi, derived from an unknown term + Latin hodiē (“today”). Compare Ligurian ancheu.

parole.significato: either of the three judges, in the old Venetian republic, who were in charge of judicial and constitutional matters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan avogadore, from Latin advocātōrem.

parole.significato: title and function borne by an envoy of the Most Serene Republic of Venice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan bailo, ultimately from Latin baiulus. Doublet of balivo and balì.
Borrowed from Venetan, from Latin calamus. Doublet of calamo.

parole.significato: a covered shelter for boats (typical of Venice and the Veneto)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan cavana, from Late Latin cabanna, capanna. Doublet of capanna.

Borrowed from Venetan s-ciao, sciavo (“slave”) (in particular the expression s-ciao vostro (literally “(I am) your slave”), in essence meaning "I am at your service", or "your humble servant"), from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”) (whence also standard Italian schiavo); in the Venetan language orig

parole.significato: dukedom, duchy (of a Venetian doge), dogate
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Venetan dogado, from Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of Latin dux (“duke; leader”) + -ātus. Compare ducato and dogato.

parole.significato: dogaressa, dogess (the wife of a doge)
parole.testo: Venetan dogaresa, from Medieval Latin ducarissa, from Latin ducatrix, from dux (“ruler”) + -issa (feminine suffix), with an additional infix. By surface analysis, doge + -essa. Doublet of duchessa.

parole.significato: dukedom, duchy (of a Venetian doge), dogate
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing from Venetan dogado, from Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of Latin dux (“duke; leader”) + -ātus. By surface analysis, doge + -ato. Doublet of ducato and dogado.
Borrowed from Venetan doxe, from Latin ducem (“leader; commander; ruler”). Doublet of duce and duca.
Borrowed from Venetan, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *cancricula, diminutive of Classical Latin cancer (“crab”).
Borrowed from Venetan lovo (“wolf”), from Latin lupus. Doublet of lupo and lupus.

parole.significato: blotched picarel (Spicara maena, a fish of the Mediterranean and Atlantic)
parole.testo: From a Venetan dialect term derived from a diminutive of Latin maena.

parole.significato: sluggish, listless, depressed, downcast, disheartened, crestfallen, dejected
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Venetan mogio (“soaked, damp”), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“to soak”), from Latin mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: a type of Venetian street sign painted directly on the plaster of walls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan niçiołeto, nisiołeto, a diminutive of niçioło, nisioło (“cloth; bedsheet”), from Latin linteolum (“linen cloth”). By surface analysis, lenzuolo + -etto.

parole.significato: unwanted air bubble which forms inside glass
parole.testo: Borrowed from Venetan pùłega (literally “flea”), used by Venetian glassmakers such as those from Murano. The term is from Vulgar Latin *pūlica (“flea”), from Latin pūlex, from Proto-Indo-European *plus-. Doublet of pulce.
Borrowed from Venetan regatar, possibly from Vulgar Latin *recaptāre.
